name: Cold compress / chilled washcloth

card.summary: A chilled cloth or pack held on the eyes to reduce morning puffiness; cold therapy has broader evidence, but not for eyes specifically.
card.aka: Cold compress, chilled spoons, ice pack
card.note: Avoid direct ice on skin; cold injury is documented in cold therapy devices.

quick.overview:
A cold compress or chilled washcloth is a simple way people try to reduce puffiness around the eyes. The cold is said to narrow vessels and limit fluid.

Cold therapy has been studied for injury and post-surgical swelling, with mixed results, but no trial was found on cosmetic under-eye puffiness.
quick.mechanism: Cold lowers tissue temperature and causes vasoconstriction; compression limits fluid leaking from vessels. In sustained cold, a cycle of vasoconstriction followed by vasodilation can occur.
quick.risks: Ice applied directly to skin can cause a cold burn, and uncontrolled cooling devices have been linked to frostbite and severe tissue damage. A cloth barrier is described as safer.

lead: A cold compress or chilled washcloth is a home practice of holding a cold, damp cloth, gel pack or chilled spoons against the closed eyes, typically after waking, to make the eye area look less puffy. The goal is a flatter lower lid and fresher, more awake-looking eyes within minutes, for example before work, photos or events.

Periorbital puffiness is swelling around the eyes caused almost always by fluid build-up, and is often worst on waking because fluid shifts while lying flat.[2] Wikipedia lists applying a cold compress near the eye for short-term relief among its suggested measures, explaining that cold narrows blood vessels and reduces fluid leakage.[2] More generally, cold lowers tissue temperature and constricts vessels, while compression limits fluid leakage.[1]

Cold therapy is used for pain and swelling after soft-tissue injury and some surgeries, including facial surgery, where a meta-analysis found it decreased pain and swelling on days two or three.[1] Evidence for cryotherapy is mixed in other settings; one systematic review found insufficient evidence in ankle sprains.[1] Randomized trials have also examined cold compresses in third-molar surgery recovery, in allergic conjunctivitis and in induced bruising, but no trial of cold compresses for cosmetic under-eye puffiness has been published.[3][4][5]

chain: Cold, damp cloth held on closed eyes
Blood vessels constrict and fluid leakage is limited
Eyelid and under-eye swelling look reduced
Eyes look fresher and less puffy
angle.text: People hold a chilled cloth or pack against the eyes for a few minutes to reduce morning puffiness, a quick routine used before leaving the house or being photographed.

infobox: Chilled cloth, gel pack, chilled spoons
Head elevation during sleep; lifestyle changes[2]

paras: Puffy lids and under-eye bags are caused mainly by fluid, and Wikipedia lists contributing factors including lying flat, ageing, allergies, crying (salt in tears may promote fluid retention), sleep loss, high dietary sodium, alcohol and tobacco, and fluid changes in pregnancy and the menstrual cycle.[2] Cold compresses are a short-term measure suggested alongside head elevation during sleep and lifestyle changes.[2]

The same article distinguishes this fluid swelling from the suborbicularis oculi fat pad beneath the lower lid, which tends to enlarge with age as the overlying muscle thins, so lids look baggy over time.[2] Because a compress acts on fluid rather than this fat pad, the visible change from a compress is described as temporary.[2]

Chilled spoons, refrigerated gel eye masks, damp cloths and ice packs wrapped in cloth are all used for the same purpose; they differ mainly in how long they stay cold and how much pressure they apply.[1]

Cold compression combines cryotherapy with static compression: cold lowers tissue temperature and slows metabolism, while compression applies pressure that limits fluid leaking from vessels.[1] Wikipedia describes a hunting reaction, a cycle of alternating constriction and dilation of blood vessels, that may begin after about 10 minutes at roughly 9.5 degrees Celsius or below, and says whether this response helps or harms recovery is debated.[1] Whether brief eye-area use produces visible changes has not been formally studied.

sections.h: Wider medical use of cold compresses
paras: A systematic review of clinical practice guidelines for conjunctivitis found that guidelines consistently recommended non-pharmacological measures including cold compress and artificial tears for non-infectious conjunctivitis.[6] A randomized trial of nonpharmacologic treatments for acute seasonal allergic conjunctivitis tested measures of this kind,[4] and a randomized trial compared cold compress with dexamethasone and ketoprofen after impacted lower third molar surgery.[3] A randomized comparison of bruise-reduction treatments used pulsed dye laser-induced bruises.[5]

sections.h: When puffiness has a medical cause
paras: Wikipedia notes that puffiness is usually a temporary cosmetic concern but that severe or persistent swelling can signal other conditions, listing periorbital cellulitis, allergic angioedema, hypothyroidism and nephrotic syndrome among those that warrant evaluation.[2] The article advises seeking medical care in such cases.[2]

Direct ice on skin can cause a cryoburn, and most ice wraps include a protective layer; refreezable gel wraps are described as safer because they stay within recommended icing times.[1] Continuous cooling machines have led to reported frostbite and, in severe cases, tissue damage requiring amputation, and are the subject of class action lawsuits.[1]

No studies found on cold compresses for under-eye puffiness. Related research includes a meta-analysis reporting that cold compression after facial surgery reduces pain and swelling on days two or three,[1] a randomized trial comparing dexamethasone, ketoprofen and cold compress after impacted lower third molar surgery,[3] a randomized trial of nonpharmacologic treatments for seasonal allergic conjunctivitis,[4] and a randomized comparison of bruise-reduction treatments after laser-induced bruising.[5]
